title: Chapter 10 — Why The Americans Are More Addicted To Practical Than To Theoretical Science
paragraphs: If a democratic state of society and democratic institutions do not halt the course of the human mind, they undeniably steer it in one direction rather than another. Their effects, though limited in this way, are still very great, and I hope I may be forgiven for pausing a moment to examine them. When we spoke of the philosophical method of the American people, we made several observations that must be put to use here.

Equality gives man the desire to judge everything for himself. It gives him, in all things, a taste for the tangible and the real, and a contempt for tradition and for forms. These general tendencies show up especially in the particular subject of this chapter. Those who cultivate the sciences among a democratic people are always afraid of losing their way in visionary speculation. They distrust systems. They hold closely to facts, and to the study of facts with their own senses. Since they do not easily defer to the mere name of any fellow man, they are never inclined to rest on anyone’s authority. On the contrary, they work tirelessly to point out the weak points in their neighbors’ opinions. Scientific precedents carry very little weight with them. They are never held up for long by the subtleties of the schools, and they are not ready to accept big words as sterling coin. They penetrate as far as they can into the main parts of the subject that occupies them, and they explain those parts in everyday language. Scientific pursuits then follow a freer and safer course, but a less lofty one.

The mind may, it seems to me, divide science into three parts. The first comprises the most theoretical principles and the more abstract notions, whose application is either unknown or very remote. The second consists of those general truths that still belong to pure theory but nevertheless lead by a straight, short road to practical results. The third is made up of methods of application and means of execution. Each of these portions of science may be cultivated separately, although reason and experience show that none of them can flourish for long if it is entirely cut off from the other two.

In America the purely practical part of science is admirably understood, and careful attention is paid to the portion of theory that is immediately needed for application. In this the Americans always show a clear, free, original, and inventive power of mind. But hardly anyone in the United States devotes himself to the essentially theoretical and abstract part of human knowledge. In this respect the Americans carry to excess a tendency that I think can be seen, though to a lesser degree, among all democratic nations.

Nothing is more necessary to the cultivation of the higher sciences, or of the more elevated branches of science, than meditation, and nothing is less suited to meditation than the structure of democratic society. There we do not find, as among an aristocratic people, one class that clings to repose because it is well off, and another that does not dare to stir because it despairs of improving its condition. Everyone is actively in motion, some in pursuit of power, others of gain. In the midst of this universal tumult, this incessant clash of conflicting interests, this continual rush of men after fortune, where is the calm to be found that the deeper workings of the intellect require? How can the mind dwell on any single point when everything whirls around it, and when man himself is swept and battered onward by the headlong current that carries everything along with it? But the permanent agitation that exists in the heart of a peaceable and established democracy must be distinguished from the tumultuous, revolutionary movements that almost always accompany the birth and growth of democratic society. When a violent revolution occurs among a highly civilized people, it cannot fail to give a sudden impulse to their feelings and their opinions. This is especially true of democratic revolutions, which stir up all the classes that make up a people and at the same time produce an immoderate ambition in the breast of every member of the community. The French made most surprising advances in the exact sciences at the very time when they were finishing the destruction of the remains of their former feudal society. Yet this sudden fertility should not be attributed to democracy, but to the unprecedented revolution that accompanied its growth. What happened at that time was a special incident, and it would be unwise to take it as the test of a general principle. Great revolutions are not more common among democratic nations than among others. I am even inclined to believe that they are less common. But among these populations there prevails a small, distressing motion, a kind of incessant jostling of men, which annoys and disturbs the mind without exciting or elevating it. Men who live in democratic communities not only seldom indulge in meditation, but they naturally hold it in very little esteem. A democratic state of society and democratic institutions plunge most men into constant active life, and the habits of mind suited to an active life are not always suited to a contemplative one. The man of action is often obliged to settle for the best he can get, because he would never achieve his purpose if he insisted on carrying every detail to perfection. He constantly has to rely on ideas that he has not had the leisure to search to the bottom. He is much more often helped by the timeliness of an idea than by its strict accuracy, and in the long run he risks less by using some false principles than by spending his time establishing all his principles on the basis of truth. The world is not led by long or learned demonstrations. A rapid glance at particular events, the daily study of the fleeting passions of the multitude, the accidents of the moment, and the art of turning them to account decide all its affairs.

In ages when active life is the condition of almost everyone, men are therefore generally led to put an excessive value on the quick flashes and superficial conceptions of the intellect, and, on the other hand, to rate its slower and deeper labors far below their true worth. This opinion of the public influences the judgment of the men who cultivate the sciences. They are persuaded that they can succeed in those pursuits without meditation, or they are deterred from the pursuits that require it.

There are several ways of studying the sciences. Among a multitude of men you will find a selfish, mercantile, trading taste for the discoveries of the mind, which must not be confused with the disinterested passion that is kindled in the hearts of a few. A desire to make use of knowledge is one thing. The pure desire to know is another. I do not doubt that in a few minds, scattered far apart, an ardent, inexhaustible love of truth springs up, sustains itself, and lives in ceaseless enjoyment without ever reaching the satisfaction it seeks. It is this ardent love, this proud, disinterested love of what is true, that raises men to the abstract sources of truth, to draw their mother-knowledge from there. If Pascal had had nothing in view but some large gain, or even if he had been driven by the love of fame alone, I cannot imagine that he would ever have been able to rally all the powers of his mind, as he did, to discover more fully the most hidden things of the Creator. When I see him, as it were, tear his soul away from all the cares of life to devote it wholly to these researches, and, snapping prematurely the links that bind the body to life, die of old age before forty, I stand amazed, and I see that no ordinary cause is at work to produce such extraordinary efforts.

The future will show whether these passions, at once so rare and so productive, come into being and grow as easily in democratic communities as in aristocratic ones. For myself, I confess that I am slow to believe it. In aristocratic society, the class that sets the tone of opinion and holds the supreme direction of affairs is placed permanently and hereditarily above the multitude. It naturally forms a lofty idea of itself and of man. It loves to invent noble pleasures for him and to carve out splendid objects for his ambition. Aristocracies often commit very tyrannical and very inhuman actions, but they rarely entertain base thoughts, and they show a kind of haughty contempt for petty pleasures, even while they indulge in them. The effect is greatly to raise the general pitch of society. In aristocratic ages, people commonly hold vast ideas of the dignity, the power, and the greatness of man. These opinions influence those who cultivate the sciences as well as the rest of the community. They help the mind’s natural impulse toward the highest regions of thought, and they naturally prepare it to conceive a sublime, even almost divine, love of truth. Men of science at such times are consequently carried away by theory, and it even happens that they often conceive a thoughtless contempt for the practical part of learning. “Archimedes,” says Plutarch, “was of so lofty a spirit that he never condescended to write any treatise on the manner of constructing all these engines of offense and defense. And as he held this science of inventing and putting together engines, and all arts generally speaking which tended to any useful end in practice, to be vile, low, and mercenary, he spent his talents and his studious hours in writing of those things only whose beauty and subtlety had in them no admixture of necessity.” Such is the aristocratic aim of science. In democratic nations it cannot be the same.

Most of the men who make up these nations are extremely eager in the pursuit of actual, physical gratification. Since they are always dissatisfied with the position they hold and always free to leave it, they think of nothing but the means of changing their fortune or increasing it. To minds so disposed, every new method that leads by a shorter road to wealth, every machine that spares labor, every instrument that lowers the cost of production, and every discovery that makes pleasures easier or increases them seems the grandest effort of the human intellect. It is chiefly from these motives that a democratic people takes up scientific pursuits, understands them, and respects them. In aristocratic ages, science is called upon above all to provide gratification to the mind. In democracies, it is called upon to provide it to the body. You may be sure that the more democratic, educated, and free a nation is, the greater will be the number of these promoters of scientific genius who act out of interest, and the more discoveries that can be applied at once to productive industry will bring gain, fame, and even power to their authors. For in democracies the working class takes part in public affairs, and public honors, as well as financial rewards, may be given to those who deserve them. In a community organized in this way, it is easy to see that the human mind may be led, without noticing, to neglect theory, and that it is driven, on the contrary, with unparalleled vehemence toward the applications of science, or at least toward that portion of theoretical science which is necessary to those who make such applications. In vain will some innate inclination raise the mind toward the loftier spheres of the intellect: interest draws it down to the middle zone. There it can develop all its energy and restless activity, and there it can produce all its wonders. These very Americans, who have not discovered a single one of the general laws of mechanics, have introduced into navigation an engine that is changing the face of the world.

Assuredly I do not contend that the democratic nations of our time are destined to see the great luminaries of man’s intelligence go out, or even that no new lights will ever appear. At the age the world has now reached, and among so many cultivated nations, all perpetually fired by the fever of productive industry, the bonds that connect the different parts of science cannot fail to strike the observer. And the taste for practical science itself, if it is educated, ought to lead men not to neglect theory. Amid such countless attempted applications of so many experiments, repeated every day, it is almost impossible that general laws should not often be brought to light, so that great discoveries would be frequent, though great inventors might be rare. I believe, moreover, in the high calling of scientific minds. If the democratic principle does not, on the one hand, lead men to cultivate science for its own sake, on the other hand it enormously increases the number of those who do cultivate it. Nor is it credible that, among so great a multitude, no speculative genius should arise from time to time, inflamed by the love of truth alone. Such a person, we may be sure, would dive into the deepest mysteries of nature, whatever the spirit of his country or his age. He needs no help in his course. It is enough that he is not hindered in it.

All I mean to say is this: permanent inequality of conditions leads men to confine themselves to the arrogant and sterile search for abstract truths, while the social condition and the institutions of democracy prepare them to seek the immediate, useful, practical results of the sciences. This tendency is natural and inevitable. It is worth knowing about, and it may be necessary to point it out. If those who are called upon to guide the nations of our time clearly saw from afar these new tendencies, which will soon be irresistible, they would understand that men living in democratic ages, possessing education and freedom, cannot fail to improve the industrial part of science, and that from now on all the efforts of the constituted authorities ought to be directed to supporting the highest branches of learning and to fostering the nobler passion for science itself. In the present age the human mind must be forced into theoretical studies. It runs of its own accord to practical applications, and instead of perpetually sending it back to the minute examination of secondary effects, it is good sometimes to turn it away from them, in order to raise it to the contemplation of primary causes. Because the civilization of ancient Rome perished as a result of the invasion of the barbarians, we are perhaps too ready to think that civilization cannot perish in any other way. If the light by which we are guided is ever extinguished, it will dwindle by degrees and die out of itself. By sticking closely to mere applications, people would lose sight of principles. When the principles were wholly forgotten, the methods derived from them would be badly pursued. New methods could no longer be invented, and men would go on applying, without intelligence and without art, scientific processes that were no longer understood.

Three hundred years ago, when Europeans first reached China, they found that nearly all the arts had attained a certain degree of perfection there. They were surprised that a people who had come so far had never gone further. Later they found some traces of the higher branches of science, which had been lost. The nation was wrapped up in productive industry. Most of its scientific processes had been kept, but science itself no longer existed. That explained the strangely motionless state in which they found the Chinese mind. The Chinese, following in their forefathers’ footsteps, had forgotten the reasons that had guided those forefathers. They still used the formula without asking what it meant. They kept the instrument, but they had lost the art of altering or renewing it. The Chinese, then, had lost the power of change, and improvement was impossible for them. At all times and in all things they had to imitate their predecessors, for fear that by straying for a moment from the path laid down for them they would wander into total darkness. The source of human knowledge was almost dry. The stream still flowed, but it could neither swell its waters nor change its course. Even so, China had lasted in peace for centuries. The invaders who had conquered the country had taken on the customs of its inhabitants, and order prevailed. A kind of physical prosperity was visible everywhere. Revolutions were rare, and war was, so to speak, unknown.

It is therefore a delusion to comfort ourselves with the thought that the barbarians are still far from us. For if some nations allow civilization to be torn from their grasp, there are others who trample it underfoot themselves.
